dossier.public_summary: The 1.66-day dip lines up exactly with the star's 1.66-day spot period and the light curve swings about 4% outside the dips with a huge phase-curve signal. The measured 'transit' depth halves from about 6,000 to 3,000 ppm over years, as spots move across the M-dwarf, not a steady planet. Centroid confirms the dip is on the target, so it is stellar variability synchronized to rotation, not a transiting planet.

reasons.why: Signal period equals stellar rotation period (signal_over_rotation=0.9995599758890897) with huge 4% spot modulation that also produces a ~4000 ppm phase curve. High-amplitude rotational modulation at the same period plus phase_curve far from zero points to spots or a close binary synchronised to spin, not a planet punching through a muted spot pattern.

reasons.why: Depth is not stable; it truly changes from ~6000 ppm in sectors 14-26 to ~3000 ppm later, inconsistent with a constant planetary transit depth on a single star. Spot activity explains the apparent 'depth' change as varying contamination of the transit shape by spots.

reasons.why: On-target difference imaging rules out a neighbour's eclipse, so the alternative is stellar variability, not a blended EB.

Flat bottom and no odd/even or secondary argue against a blended EB, but a small-star or grazing planetary eclipse can also look flat; together with the period/equal-to-rotation and phase_curve evidence the flat shape is best explained by spots creating a pseudo-flat dip at the rotational phase, not a planet.
